The Yukon River. Flowing approximately one thousand nine hundred eighty miles through western Canada and Alaska from the Whitehorse region of the Yukon Territory northwestward to the Bering Sea, the Yukon is one of North America's longest rivers. It drains a vast subarctic and arctic region and has been central to indigenous life, the Klondike Gold Rush, and modern Alaskan geography. The river originates near Whitehorse in the Yukon Territory of Canada and flows northwestward across the territory before entering Alaska. It passes through Dawson City, the site of the Klondike Gold Rush of the eighteen nineties, which brought thousands of prospectors seeking gold along its banks and tributaries. The name comes from a native Athabaskan word Youcon or Ykon, meaning great river. The Yukon freezes completely in winter and becomes the primary transportation corridor for indigenous peoples and explorers during the brief summer season. The river flows through wilderness largely untouched by development for most of its course, with a landscape that ranges from boreal forest to tundra. It discharges into the Bering Sea near the Alaska-Russia maritime boundary and has historically been important for salmon fisheries and indigenous subsistence. The river and its valleys contain unique subarctic ecosystems with wildlife including moose, grizzly bears, and migratory caribou herds that inhabit the vast interior of the far north.
